UNIT 26: DEVELOPMENT - INDICATORS, MODELS AND INEQUALITY

KEY THEME
- Development models and measures are tools that help us understand how countries improve lives, grow economically and care for people and the environment.

LEARNING OUTCOMES (3.9, 3.10)
- Describe protectionism, modernisation and sustainable development as approaches to development.
- Assess strengths and limitations of GDP, GNP/GNI, the Human Development Index (HDI) and the Gender Development Index (GDI).
- Describe the three parts of the HDI: a long and healthy life, access to education, a reasonable standard of living.
- Explain the factors that affect each part of the HDI.
- Compare how factors affect HDI in Ireland and Afghanistan.

APPROACH 1: PROTECTIONISM
- Protectionism: when a government restricts and limits international trade.
- Tools: tariffs (taxes on imported goods), quotas (limits on the amount that can be imported) and subsidies (government financial support for local businesses).
- These make imports dearer or harder to get, so consumers buy local goods, helping domestic industries grow.
- Short term: protects jobs and promotes home-grown industry.
- Long term: consumers may pay more and economic efficiency may fall.
- Example: the US. Import tariffs make goods from China and Europe more expensive. Tariffs on steel imports helped the US steel industry by encouraging people to buy US-made steel.
- Problems: other countries retaliate with their own tariffs, creating trade wars. US businesses importing materials face higher costs, consumers pay more, and global trade becomes less steady and harder to predict.
- Figure 26.1 is a political cartoon depicting protectionism.

APPROACH 2: MODERNISATION
- Modernisation theory: if less economically developed countries (LEDCs) copy more economically developed countries (MEDCs) by abandoning traditional methods and investing in modern technology, industry and education, they will become wealthier.
- Development happens in stages: poor countries begin very traditional and slow to change; they gain new ideas such as modern farming; they become less rural and more urbanised; towns and cities grow with industry and better education.
- Urbanisation: the growth of towns and cities.
- Criticism: every country is unique; what works for some does not work for all.
- Example: China, moving from a rural, agricultural country to a world leader in technology, industry and urbanisation. Huge investment in robotics and engineering. Job creation caused large-scale rural-to-urban migration, e.g. to Shenzhen (Figures 26.2 and 26.3 show Shenzhen in 1982 and today).
- Success: China is a global leader in industrial output and many people have been lifted out of poverty.
- Problems: economic inequality (unequal distribution of wealth and opportunity) between poorer rural and wealthier urban areas; environmental pressures from overcrowding and rapid city growth.
- Figure 26.4: Beijing had 77,000 cars and 5.6 million bikes in 1978, but 83.54 million cars (as given in the figure) and 2 million (shared) bikes in 2018. This shows a shift to car transport as the country modernised.

APPROACH 3: SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
- Aims to improve quality of life by solving current problems like hunger, poverty and pollution without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
- Three pillars (interconnected, so solutions should help all three):
- Environmental: protecting the environment (clean air, water and forests).
- Economic: building a stable economy (jobs and businesses).
- Social: fairness and equity in society (reducing poverty, meeting everyone's needs).
- Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): worldwide targets including ending poverty, fighting climate change and ensuring clean water and good health for everyone.
- Example: Finland ranked first on the 2025 SDG Index. It balances economic growth with environmental protection and social equity, prioritising waste recycling, clean transport, health and education.
- Figure 26.7: Finland aims to be carbon neutral in 2035 (Finnish Ministry of the Environment), using emission cuts and actions to strengthen carbon sinks.

POSITIVES AND NEGATIVES OF THE APPROACHES
- Protectionism keeps local businesses safe but can mean less choice and higher prices.
- Modernisation offers a clear path to becoming more advanced but can ignore what makes each country special and can damage the environment.
- Sustainable development balances nature, people and money but takes time and is harder to put into practice.
- Choosing an approach is hard because every country is unique. Leaders consider wealth, education levels, natural resources and which problems (poverty, pollution, unemployment) need solving.
- Example: a country with lots of farmland might modernise agriculture; a country with environmental problems might prioritise sustainable development.
- Goal: improve living standards, promote fairness and protect the environment for now and the future.

MEASURES OF DEVELOPMENT
- Four key measures: Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Income (GNI), Human Development Index (HDI) and Gender Development Index (GDI).
- Purchasing Power Parity (PPP): a way to compare the value of money between countries by comparing what the same amount of money can buy.

GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT (GDP)
- The total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country, including foreign-owned industries based there.
- Includes goods such as medicines, technology, food and clothes, and services that are paid for. Does not include voluntary work.
- High GDP: economy growing, producing and selling more. Low GDP: shrinking economy.
- Calculated by adding what people spend, what businesses invest, what government spends and what the country sells abroad, minus what it buys from abroad.
- Every country calculates it the same way, so economies are easy to compare.
- Used by governments to decide on infrastructure, taxes and planning (e.g. build more roads if GDP rises; worry about unemployment if it falls). Banks use it to set interest rates (the cost of borrowing).
- Nominal GDP: total value of goods and services in a year at current prices; does not account for inflation.
- GDP at PPP: adjusts for things costing more in some places (e.g. a burger costing €2 in one country and €6 in another).
- GDP per capita: total GDP divided by population. If two countries have the same GDP but one has twice the people, people in the smaller country are on average better off.
- Worked example: GDP €2 trillion and population 100 million gives GDP per capita of €2,000,000,000,000 / 100,000,000 = €20,000.
- Figure 26.8 shows the world's top 10 economies from 1992 to 2024 (World Bank and IMF).
STRENGTHS OF GDP
- A clear, simple number; shows how much money a country has earned.
- Allows comparison of economic development between countries.
- Rising GDP usually means a booming economy, more jobs and profits.
- Globally accepted, so everyone uses the same data.
LIMITATIONS OF GDP
- Shows total money but not who has it; it can rise when only a few wealthy people earn more.
- Does not measure health, wellbeing or environmental costs such as water and air pollution.
- Excludes unpaid work like volunteering or caring for family.
- Excludes the informal economy (activity outside formal workplaces and income tax, e.g. casual labour, street vending, cash-in-hand odd jobs), important in developing countries (e.g. street vendors in Nigeria).

GROSS NATIONAL INCOME (GNI)
- GNI per capita: the total value of goods and services produced by a country's people and home-grown businesses at home, plus income received from its people and businesses abroad. (In the summary table: GDP plus income earned by citizens/businesses abroad.)
- High GNI per capita means more developed.
- Geofact: Glanbia, an Irish multinational nutrition company headquartered in Kilkenny, has over 5,500 employees in more than 30 countries and sells in over 130 countries.
STRENGTHS OF GNI
- Counts all income of a country's people and businesses at home and abroad (e.g. an Irish person abroad sending money home, or an Irish firm's overseas profits).
- Wider picture than GDP because not limited to borders.
- Shows the importance of remittances (money sent home) in countries like India and the Philippines.
- Identifies countries with globally successful businesses (MNCs).
LIMITATIONS OF GNI
- Does not show how wealth is divided or inequality between rich and poor.
- Can be very high where a few multinationals make huge profits abroad that do not benefit ordinary families.
- Exchange rates and cost of living distort it (e.g. €5 buys more in Afghanistan than in Ireland).
- Ignores informal work (babysitting, farm labour paid in cash). In sub-Saharan Africa over 85% of jobs are informal.
- Does not measure quality of life or happiness: GNI may rise in Bangladesh or Poland because people emigrate and send remittances, but families are split up and young people forced to leave (Figure 26.10: Bangladeshi migrant workers sharing a room in Lebanon).

HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI)
- A scoring system developed by the United Nations to rank countries on social and economic conditions; a more rounded measure.
- Three dimensions and indicators:
- Long and healthy life: life expectancy at birth (life expectancy index).
- Knowledge/education: mean years of schooling for adults (aged 25+) and expected years of schooling for children (education index).
- Decent standard of living: GNI per capita (PPP $) (GNI index).
- Score between 0 and 1; closer to 1 means more developed.
STRENGTHS OF HDI
- Looks at health, education and quality of life as well as wealth, giving a better overall picture of how good lives are.
- A country with good schools and hospitals can score highly even if it is not the wealthiest.
- Governments and organisations use it to identify problem areas and plan solutions (e.g. comparing Ireland and Afghanistan shows differences in daily life, not just wealth).
LIMITATIONS OF HDI
- One average figure can hide inequalities between regions.
- Leaves out environment, pollution, political freedom, personal safety and fair treatment regardless of gender or background.
- Based on statistics submitted by each country; may be inaccurate in war or if a government is dishonest.
- Does not measure happiness directly; two countries with the same score may feel very different to live in.

GENDER DEVELOPMENT INDEX (GDI)
- Measures differences in HDI achievements between men and women in health, education and income.
- A score of 1 means perfect gender parity (equality).
STRENGTHS OF GDI
- Compares opportunities for men and women; identifies unfair gaps (e.g. girls attending fewer years of school, women dying younger).
- High GDI: boys and girls have the same chance of long healthy lives, education and income.
- Helps governments and the UN plan solutions, e.g. programmes to keep girls in school or labour laws to close the pay gap.
LIMITATIONS OF GDI
- Uses national averages; ignores regional or ethnic differences. Example: 2016 census, 13% of Traveller girls in Ireland were educated to secondary level compared with 69% of the general population; GDI would not show this.
- Only compares males and females; says nothing about challenges facing groups like LGBTQ+ people.
- Leaves out discrimination, personal safety, political and cultural freedom and happiness.
- Some countries lack accurate records of women's wages or school attendance.
- Can look good even when all genders do badly (if no child goes to secondary school, all are 'equal').
- Must be combined with other indicators.
- SDG 5 (gender equality; empower all women and girls): end discrimination and violence against women and girls; eliminate harmful practices such as child and forced marriage and female genital mutilation; recognise unpaid care and domestic work; ensure women's full participation in leadership; universal access to sexual and reproductive health; equal rights to economic resources; promote empowerment.

USING MEASURES IN COMBINATION
- GDP and GNI show how much money a country makes but only part of the story.
- HDI and GDI add health, education and gender equality and show where groups need help.
- No single measure is perfect; use several together for a fairer picture.

WHAT SHAPES A COUNTRY'S HDI? (FIGURE 26.16, UNdata, 2023)
- Iceland: rank 1, HDI 0.972, life expectancy 82.7, expected schooling 18.9, mean schooling 13.9, GNI per capita (PPP) $69,117.
- Ireland: rank 11, HDI 0.949, life expectancy 82.4, expected schooling 19.2, mean schooling 11.7, GNI per capita $90,885.
- India: rank 130, HDI 0.685, life expectancy 72.0, expected 13.0, mean 6.9, GNI about $9,047.
- Afghanistan: rank 182, HDI 0.462, life expectancy 62.0, expected about 10.3, mean about 3.9, GNI about $1,000.
- South Sudan: rank 193, HDI 0.388, life expectancy 55.0, expected 6.0, mean 5.5, GNI about $688.
- Factors shaping HDI: physical (climate, physical landscape), economic (debt, trade), social (colonial history, conflict and peace, government policies).

CASE STUDY: IRELAND'S HDI (0.949, among the world's top nations)
Key terms
- Project Ireland 2040: the government's national spatial planning strategy.
- National Development Plan (NDP): the government's public capital investment programme for 2021-2030.
- Industrial Development Authority (IDA): agency attracting and supporting FDI in Ireland.
Physical factors
- Temperate, wet climate supports a highly productive agricultural sector, e.g. profitable export-driven dairy and beef farming in the Golden Vale of Munster.
- Climate change: repeated flooding of the River Slaney in Enniscorthy, Co. Wexford (e.g. January 2026) closed schools and destroyed homes and businesses; Storm Éowyn (2025) caused power outages and costly repairs.
- Flat, low-lying land and deep fertile soils (south and east, e.g. Co. Meath) support farming and rural living, raising incomes and food supply.
- Remote west and northwest regions (e.g. Donegal) with difficult landscapes have lower HDI: isolated or upland areas have poor access to schools, healthcare and jobs.
- Urban areas like Dublin with good infrastructure and services have higher HDI than rural regions.
Economic factors
- After the 2008 crisis Ireland had massive debt; careful management cut it from 117% of GDP (2012) to 34.9% of GDP (2025).
- This allowed investment in services, e.g. the new National Children's Hospital in Dublin and school building in fast-growing areas like west Dublin and Cork.
- Open economy dependent on trade and FDI: AbbVie in Co. Mayo (produces the world's entire supply of Botox), Intel in Co. Kildare (microchips). Ireland exported €224 billion in goods in 2024.
- Trade profits fund transport upgrades under Project Ireland 2040 and the NDP, SUSI student grants, better public transport and jobs in tech firms like Google and Facebook in Dublin's Silicon Docks.
Social factors
- British colonial rule caused centuries of economic stagnation and hardship.
- The Troubles in Northern Ireland: unsafe travel to work and school, school closures, lack of political and cultural freedom, communities insecure for generations. Higher unemployment, lower wages and poorer conditions especially in Catholic nationalist communities.
- The Good Friday Agreement (1998) gradually improved healthcare, education and living standards; peace brought trade, investment, tourism and infrastructure; HDI rose as unemployment fell.
- Government policies: free secondary education, health campaigns (school vaccination programmes), mental health investment, free schoolbooks (and lunches in primary schools), infrastructure such as Dublin MetroLink.
- IDA attracts FDI, e.g. Intel employs 4,900 in Ireland; secures thousands of jobs for graduates.
Future
- Heavy dependence on FDI makes Ireland vulnerable to US trade policy, tariffs or tech layoffs; needs more balanced, resilient policies.
- Housing crisis: shortage of social housing and high rents and prices are barriers to higher living standards; government plans more affordable housing.

CASE STUDY: AFGHANISTAN'S HDI (text gives 0.496; table gives 0.462, rank 182; among the lowest in the world)
Key terms
- Monarchy: government by a king or queen, usually inheriting power.
- Republic: people elect leaders to govern.
- Taliban rule: government by the Taliban, an Islamist group, based on a strict interpretation of sharia law, limiting freedoms especially for women and minorities. The Taliban began in Afghanistan in the mid-1990s.
Physical factors
- Dry climate with frequent droughts, unpredictable rain and extreme temperature ranges. Severe drought since 2021.
- 80% of Afghans depend on farming, so drought means less drinking water, failed crops, food shortages, malnutrition and lower life expectancy.
- Climate change worsens poverty and hunger; climate refugees disrupt children's education.
- High mountains and dry plains make transport and access to hospitals, clinics and schools hard, especially in winter; emergency healthcare almost impossible in remote areas.
- Soil erosion and desertification lower farm output and incomes; in the north, loss of grassland and failed harvests mean families lose livestock and earnings.
- Poor infrastructure (water systems, sanitation) makes recovery from disasters harder.
Economic factors
- Low debt (about 20% of GNI/GDP) but cannot borrow: government has little money and is seen as too risky to lend to because of conflict and instability, so little is invested in education and health.
- High import dependence and few exports: imports rose 39% in 2024, costing $9.7 billion; a widening budget gap; spending goes on basic needs; schools and healthcare underfunded.
- Up to 97% of Afghans live in poverty due to lack of jobs.
Social factors
- Never fully colonised, but Britain influenced borders in the 1800s. Ethnic tribal groups stayed strong, leaving a weak central government; rural areas lack hospitals, schools and infrastructure.
- Almost 2 million people have died in conflict over recent decades. The Taliban insurgency overturned the government; hospitals and schools destroyed, millions lost homes.
- Over 3 million Afghans have fled since 2001, living as refugees in neighbouring countries with poor medical care and girls often unable to attend school.
- Government changed from monarchy to republic to Taliban rule; instability kept services underfunded.
- Taliban policies closed girls' secondary schools and restricted women's university education and work. In 2023, about 3.7 million children were not in school.
Future
- Depends on peace, better access to schools and healthcare, strong fair leadership and international help.

SUMMARY TABLE
- Protectionism: limits trade (tariffs, quotas, subsidies); US; builds local industry and preserves jobs; higher prices, trade disputes.
- Modernisation: follow the steps of wealthy countries (education, technology, cities, industry); China; clear path; may ignore culture and environment, risk of inequality.
- Sustainable development: balances growth, fairness and environment; Finland; benefits people and nature; slower, hard to balance pillars.
- GDP: easy to compare, shows output; ignores quality of life, equality, environment.
- GNI: shows total income for residents; ignores distribution and quality of life.
- HDI: health, education, living standards; averages hide local differences, ignores happiness and environment.
- GDI: identifies gender inequality; ignores other inequalities, relies on averages.
- HDI factors: economic (balanced debt and open trade raise HDI), environmental (climate and landscape), social (colonial history, conflict, government policy).

rows.prompt: Explain one positive and one negative of protectionism.

rows.prompt: Name and describe the three pillars of sustainable development.
rows.model_answer: Environmental: protecting clean air, water and forests. Economic: building a stable economy with jobs and businesses. Social: fairness and equity, reducing poverty so everyone's needs are met. They are interconnected so solutions should help all three.

rows.prompt: Give two strengths and two limitations of GDP as a measure of development.
rows.model_answer: Strengths: it is a clear, simple number that is calculated the same way everywhere, so economies are easy to compare; rising GDP usually means more jobs and profits. Limitations: it does not show who has the money, so it can rise when only the rich gain; it ignores health, wellbeing, pollution, unpaid work and the informal economy.

rows.prompt: Explain why GNI might give a misleading picture of development.
rows.model_answer: GNI does not show how wealth is shared, and can be high where a few MNCs make big profits abroad that do not help ordinary families. Exchange rates and cost of living distort it (€5 buys more in Afghanistan than in Ireland). It ignores informal work and quality of life; remittances may raise GNI while families are split up.

rows.prompt: Identify the three dimensions of the HDI and how each is measured.
rows.model_answer: A long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth. Education, measured by mean years of schooling for adults aged 25+ and expected years of schooling for children. A decent standard of living, measured by GNI per capita (PPP).

rows.prompt: Explain one strength and one limitation of the Gender Development Index.
rows.model_answer: A strength is that it compares men and women in health, education and income, showing unfair gaps so governments and the UN can plan solutions like keeping girls in school. A limitation is that it uses national averages, hiding groups like Traveller girls (13% educated to secondary level vs 69%), and it can look good if all genders do badly.

rows.prompt: Explain how government policies have helped Ireland's HDI score.
rows.model_answer: Policies like free secondary education, school vaccination programmes, mental health investment and free schoolbooks improve education and health. The IDA attracts FDI, e.g. Intel employs 4,900, creating jobs. Investment such as the National Children's Hospital and Dublin MetroLink improves services and living standards.

rows.prompt: Explain how the physical landscape of Afghanistan affects its HDI.
rows.model_answer: High mountains and dry plains make it hard to reach hospitals and schools in remote areas, especially in winter, so education levels and life expectancy are lower. Soil erosion and desertification reduce farm output and incomes. Drought since 2021 causes food shortages and malnutrition for the 80% who depend on farming.

rows.prompt: Describe the key ideas of protectionism and modernisation as approaches to development, with reference to named examples. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Protectionism is when a government restricts and limits international trade. It uses tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on imports) and subsidies (support for local businesses) to make imports dearer so consumers buy local goods. This helps domestic industries grow and protects jobs in the short term. The US is an example: import tariffs on goods from China and Europe made steel imports dearer and helped the US steel industry. However, other countries retaliate, causing trade wars; US firms importing materials face higher costs and consumers pay more, and trade becomes less predictable. Modernisation theory says LEDCs will become wealthier if they copy MEDCs, abandoning traditional methods and investing in technology, industry and education. Development happens in stages, from traditional and rural to urbanised and industrial. China is an example: it invested heavily in robotics and engineering, and job creation caused rural-to-urban migration to cities like Shenzhen. It is now a global leader in industrial output and many were lifted out of poverty. In Beijing cars rose from 77,000 in 1978 while bikes fell. But critics say not every country can follow the same path, and China has inequality between rural and urban areas and environmental pressure from overcrowding.
rows.marking_scheme: Each approach: named 2m + example 2m + 5-6 SRPs x 2m. Total 15m per approach (e.g. definition, tariffs/quotas/subsidies, protects jobs, US steel, trade wars, higher prices; stages, urbanisation, China robotics, Shenzhen migration, poverty reduced, inequality, environmental pressure).

rows.prompt: Assess the strengths and limitations of using GDP and the HDI as ways of measuring development. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: GDP is the total value of all finished goods and services produced within a country, including foreign-owned firms. Strengths: it is a clear, simple number; every country calculates it the same way so economies can be compared; rising GDP usually means more jobs and profits; it is globally accepted. GDP per capita (e.g. €2 trillion / 100 million = €20,000) shows average wealth. Limitations: it does not show who holds the money, so it can rise when only a few rich people gain; it ignores health, wellbeing and pollution; it leaves out unpaid work like caring and the informal economy, such as street vendors in Nigeria. The HDI, developed by the UN, combines life expectancy, years of schooling and GNI per capita into a score from 0 to 1. Strengths: it shows health, education and living standards, not just wealth, so a country with good schools and hospitals can score well; it helps governments find problem areas, e.g. comparing Ireland (0.949) and Afghanistan. Limitations: one average figure hides regional inequality; it ignores environment, political freedom and personal safety; it relies on statistics from each country that may be inaccurate during war; and it does not measure happiness.
rows.marking_scheme: GDP: 7 SRPs x 2m; HDI: 8 SRPs x 2m (total 15 SRPs = 30m). Both strengths and limitations must be covered for full marks; max 10 SRPs on one measure.

rows.prompt: HDI is influenced by physical, economic and social factors. Compare how these factors impact human development in Ireland and Afghanistan. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Physical: Ireland's temperate, wet climate and flat fertile land support profitable dairy and beef farming in the Golden Vale, raising incomes, though remote areas like Donegal have poorer access to services and flooding on the Slaney in Enniscorthy closed schools. Afghanistan's dry climate and severe drought since 2021 hit the 80% who depend on farming, causing food shortages and malnutrition; high mountains make schools and hospitals hard to reach. Economic: Ireland cut its debt from 117% of GDP in 2012 to 34.9% in 2025, funding the National Children's Hospital and new schools; it exported €224 billion in goods in 2024 and hosts MNCs like Intel and AbbVie. Afghanistan has low debt (about 20%) but cannot borrow as it is too risky; imports rose 39% in 2024 to $9.7 billion with few exports, and up to 97% live in poverty. Social: Ireland suffered colonial rule and the Troubles, but the Good Friday Agreement (1998) brought peace and investment, and policies like free education and free schoolbooks raised HDI to 0.949. Afghanistan has had decades of conflict with almost 2 million deaths and over 3 million refugees; Taliban rule closed girls' secondary schools and 3.7 million children were out of school in 2023, keeping HDI very low.
rows.marking_scheme: Comparison across all three factor types. 15 SRPs x 2m = 30m. Max 9 SRPs on one country. Statistics and named places count as SRPs. Comparison must be explicit for full marks.

rows.prompt: Identify and describe the three main parts of the HDI. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The HDI was developed by the UN and gives each country a score from 0 to 1, where closer to 1 means more developed. The first part is a long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth, for example 82.4 years in Ireland compared with 62.0 in Afghanistan. The second part is knowledge or education, measured by the mean years of schooling of adults aged 25+ and the expected years of schooling for children starting school. Ireland's expected schooling is 19.2 years. The third part is a decent standard of living, measured by GNI per capita adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), for example $90,885 in Ireland and about $1,000 in Afghanistan.

rows.prompt: Explain two limitations of the Gender Development Index as a measure of development. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: First, the GDI uses national averages and ignores regional or ethnic differences: in 2016 only 13% of Traveller girls in Ireland were educated to secondary level compared with 69% of the population, but the GDI would not show this. Second, it can look good even when all genders do badly, for example if no child can attend secondary school, all genders are 'equal', which is not real progress.
